name: Munsar Lake and Shrines
significance: A large medieval reservoir at Viramgam ringed by small stone shrines, credited to Minaldevi, mother of the Chaulukya king Jayasimha Siddharaja, and dated to 1090. Among the shrines are pedestals thought to have held a Krishna image and basins associated with Shiva worship.

name: Kodandarama Temple, Gollala Mamidada
significance: Begun in 1889 by the local zamindar brothers Dwarampudi Subbi Reddy and Rami Reddy and rebuilt in stone by 1939, with tall gopurams added through the 1950s. Its scale and pilgrim draw have earned it the nickname Chinna Bhadradri, the little Bhadrachalam.

name: Sri Santhana Venugopala Swamy Temple, Thettu
significance: A Krishna shrine in Kurabalakota mandal whose early fabric is linked to Chola and Ganga patronage, and which the Hoysala king Veera Ballala endowed with land in 1298. The deity is invoked here as Santana Venugopala, the granter of offspring.
story: Krishna is said to have appeared in a Ganga ruler's dream; the king's chariot wheel stuck fast at the spot, and digging there revealed the image that was installed at Sage Koundinya's ashram.

name: Basudev Devalaya
significance: A Vaishnava temple in Nalbari district raised under the Ahom king Sutanphaa in the first half of the eighteenth century. It remains an active local centre of Basudev worship in lower Assam.
story: A fisherman's net is said to have stayed snagged in the Jaymangal Beel for seven days until a villager, Gada Kahar, dreamed that Basudev wished to be freed from it; when the king could not lift the stones from the spot, he built the temple over them.

name: Vazhukaruteeswarar Temple
significance: A small Shiva temple on Gandhi Road in Kanchipuram whose lingam is described as showing sixteen shades. Devotees resort to it when entangled in litigation, praying for their cases to be cleared.
story: The devas and asuras are said to have set up the lingam here while disputing the meaning of sat and asat, and Shiva appeared to settle the doubt, whence the name Vazhukaruteeswarar.

name: Rathasena Mata Temple
significance: A hilltop goddess shrine in the Maruwas area of Udaipur, reached by a walking path up the slope, housing a stone image of Rathasan Mata. It is a local devotional site rather than a monumental temple.

name: Rajacholeesvarar Temple, Thirumalairayanpattinam
deity: Rajacholeesvarar (Shiva, as a lingam); goddess Abirami
significance: A Shiva temple in Thirumalairayanpattinam, the settlement founded as the seat of Saluva Thirumalairayan, a fifteenth-century Vijayanagara representative in the Karaikal region. Its prakara carries sculptures of the sixty-three Nayanmars.

name: Kali Bari, Shimla
deity: Shyamala, a form of the goddess Kali
significance: Established in the early nineteenth century by Bengali surveyors who came to Shimla as the British built their summer capital, and run since 1902 by a temple trust. The goddess Shyamala worshipped here is one suggested source of the city's own name.

name: Nandeesvarar Temple, Nandivanam
deity: Nandeesvarar (Shiva, as a lingam); goddess Soundaranayaki
significance: A Shiva temple at Nandivaram near Guduvancheri, with the lingam of Nandeesvarar in the sanctum and a separate shrine for the goddess Soundaranayaki. It is the principal temple of the town.
story: A herdboy is said to have noticed that one cow gave its milk each day at a particular spot and came home dry; when the ground was dug there, a lingam was found rising from it.

name: Kali Temple, Visakhapatnam
significance: Built in 1984 on the Ramakrishna Beach road, this Kali temple follows the nine-spired navaratna form of the Dakshineswar temple in Kolkata. It is a landmark of the Visakhapatnam seafront and draws crowds at Vijayadashami.

name: Gandhari Amman Kovil
significance: A goddess temple at Mele Thampanoor in the Kerala capital, close to Thiruvananthapuram Central station, with subsidiary shrines to Ganesha, Muruga, the naga deities, Bhairava and the navagrahas. Its main festival is Chithra Pournami in May.

name: Someswara Swamy Temple, Appikonda
significance: An eleventh-century Shiva temple on the coast near Visakhapatnam, attributed to the Chola king Kulottunga I and known locally as the Chola monument. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India and draws very large crowds at Maha Shivaratri.

name: Talesavara Siva Temple – II
significance: A small Kalinga-style Shiva shrine of the twelfth to thirteenth century standing in the Bharati Matha precinct at Badhaibanka chowk in old Bhubaneswar, with the lingam set in a circular sanctum. The matha maintains it and has repaired cyclone damage to the structure.

name: Tara Devi Temple
deity: Tara Devi, one of the ten Mahavidyas
significance: A timber-and-stone kath kuni temple on a ridge some seven kilometres from Shimla, built by the Sen rulers around 1766 and credited to King Bhupendra Sen. It is among the best known Mahavidya shrines in the Himachal hills.
story: Bhupendra Sen is said to have been asked in a vision by the goddess Tara to enshrine her, and a later king, Balbir Sen, was told in a similar vision to place the temple on the Tarav hilltop where it stands.

name: Gangeshwar Mahadev Temple
significance: A shore shrine near Fudam village on Diu where five Shiva lingas of different sizes stand among rocks at the tide line, submerged at high tide and exposed at low. The name is read as Ganga plus Ishwar, for the Shiva who received the descending Ganga in his hair.
story: The five lingas are said to have been carved and worshipped by the Pandavas while they were living in disguise during their exile.

name: Rajarajeswaramudaiya Mahadevar Temple
deity: Rajarajeswaramudaiya Mahadevar (Shiva), also called Theerthapaleeswarar; consort Kamakshi Amman
significance: A tenth-century Shiva temple at Sivapuram built under Rajaraja Chola and extended by his son Rajendra Chola I, now cared for by the Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology. Its walls carry a dense body of Chola inscriptions, including a grant by Rajendra I of 180 goats to keep two perpetual lamps burning.

name: Shyama Mai Temple
significance: Built in 1933 by Maharaja Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga on the cremation site of his father Maharaja Rameshwar Singh, this Kali temple is among the most visited shrines in Mithila.
story: The dark form worshipped here is explained by the episode in which the goddess turned black with fury after Rama slew Sahastraanan, and grew calm and abashed only when her foot came to rest on Shiva's chest.

name: Laxminrusingha Temple
significance: A Kalinga-style Narasimha temple in Purbakachha village in the Salipur area of Cuttack district. Its principal observances are Nrusingha Chaturdashi and Dola Purnima.

name: Harimukteesvarar Temple, Ariyamangai
deity: Harimukteesvarar (Shiva, as a metre-high lingam); goddess Gnanambikai Amman
significance: A modest Shiva temple with a small vimana and no gopura, standing about ten kilometres from Chakkarapalli on the Thanjavur–Kumbakonam road. It is one of the seven Saptamangai shrines of the Matrikas, and holds five saptamatrika figures of the ninth century and a Dakshinamurthy of the thirteenth.
story: Vishnu is said to have worshipped the lingam here, and from Hari, a name of Vishnu, the deity is called Harimukteesvarar.

name: Tribeniswar Temple
significance: A Kalinga-style Shiva temple at Chasakhanda in the Mahanga block, about thirty-three kilometres north-east of Cuttack city off National Highway 5. Mahashivratri and Kartik Purnima are its principal festivals.

name: Siddheshwar Temple, Toka
deity: Shiva (large lingam, with Parvati on the rear wall)
significance: A twelfth- to thirteenth-century Seuna (Yadava) temple complex of three shrines, to Shiva, Vishnu and the Devi, with later additions from the Peshwa period. Its walls carry a dense programme of carvings drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranas.

name: Shrimant Bhausaheb Rangari Ganapati Temple
significance: The Ganesha installed here in 1892 by Bhausaheb Lakshman Jawle, known as Shrimant Bhausaheb Rangari, was the focus of India's first sarvajanik or public Ganesh celebration. The wood-and-bran idol shows Ganesha slaying a demon, an image the freedom-fighter founder intended as the victory of good over evil.

name: Gurdwara Guptsar Sahib
deity: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru
significance: A gurdwara at Chhattiana marking the visit of Guru Gobind Singh to the village after the Battle of Muktsar in 1705. The shrine of the recluse Ibrahim, whom the Guru is said to have named Ajmer Singh, stands to its north-west.

name: Gurdwara Karamsar Rara Sahib
deity: Named for Sant Karam Singh; the village was sanctified by Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru
significance: Founded in 1936 after Sant Isher Singh and Sant Kishen Singh settled at Rara at the request of Sardar Gian Singh Rarewala, on land bought and partly donated by neighbouring villagers. It takes its name from Sant Karam Singh of Hoti Mardan.
story: The village is said to have become Rara Sahib, rather than plain Rara, after the sixth Guru, Hargobind Sahib, visited it.

name: Gurdwara Manji Sahib, Alamgir
deity: Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru
significance: A historic gurdwara near the village of Alamgir in Ludhiana district, marking a place where Guru Gobind Singh stayed briefly.

name: Gurdwara Naulakha Sahib
deity: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru, and Mata Gujri
significance: Established in 1830 in Naulakha village, roughly thirteen kilometres from Sirhind, to commemorate a visit by Guru Tegh Bahadur and Mata Gujri.
story: Lakhi Shah Wanjara, having lost an ox, is said to have vowed an offering to Guru Tegh Bahadur; when the animal returned he gave nine takas, which the Guru declared equal to nine lakh, and told the villagers to call the place Naulakha.

name: Vedadri Narasimha Temple
significance: A hill temple on the Krishna river housing five forms of Narasimha, counted among the Pancha Narasimha Kshetras. It was patronised under the Kakatiya empire and renovated in the nineteenth century by Raja Vasireddy Muktiswara Prasad Nayudu.
story: The demon Somakasura is said to have stolen the Vedas and hidden them in the ocean, whereupon Vishnu took the form of Narasimha to recover them and turned them into the hill of Vedadri beside the Krishna.

name: Shanti Stupa, Leh
deity: Relics of the Buddha, enshrined at the base by the 14th Dalai Lama
significance: A white peace pagoda above Chanspa in Leh, begun in 1983 under the Japanese monk Bhikshu Gyomyo Nakamura and finished in 1991, with relics of the Buddha installed at its base by the 14th Dalai Lama, who inaugurated the foundation in 1985. Built by the Ladakh Shanti Stupa Committee with Japanese and Indian support and the backing of Kushok Bakula Rinpoche, it departs deliberately from traditional Ladakhi form.

name: Deopani Durga Mandir
significance: A trust-run Durga temple at Bokajan in Karbi Anglong, built around an image dug up together with other archaeological material on the Deopani Tea Estate by its owner, the Rajput planter Surendra Nath Roy. Durga Puja is its main annual observance.

name: Mankeshwar Temple, Zodage
dynasty: Yadava or Shilahara, under Chalukya suzerainty
significance: A thirteenth-century basalt Shiva temple at Zodage in Nashik district, thought to have been raised by the Yadavas or the Shilaharas under Chalukya overlordship, with carvings of Chamunda, Bhairava and Vishnu. Mahashivratri is its chief festival and a fair is held on the thirteenth day of Magha.
